20:1: Abu Jaafar Muhammad bin Jarir said: The people of interpretation differed in the interpretation of his saying Ta Ha. Some of them said: Its meaning is, O man. Who said that? Ibn Hamid told us: Abu Tamila told us, on the authority of Al-Hasan bin Waqid, on the authority of Yazid Al-Nahwi, on the authority of Ikrimah, on the authority of Ibn Abbas: Ta-Ha 20:in Nabataean: O man. Muhammad bin Saad told me, he said: My father told me, he said: My uncle told me, he said: My father told me, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding his statement, “Ta Ha. We have not sent down the Qur’an upon you to make you miserable.” His people said, This man has been made miserable by his Lord. So God, the Most High, revealed Ta Ha, meaning: O man, We have not sent down the Qur’an upon you to make you miserable. Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, he said: Abdullah bin Muslim and Ya’la bin Muslim told me, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubayr, that he said: Ta-Ha: O man in Syriac. Ibn Jurayj said: And Zam`ah ibn Salih informed me, on the authority of Salamah ibn Wahram, on the authority of Ikrimah, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, of that as well. Ibn Jurayj said, and Mujahid said, that as well. Imran bin Musa Al-Qazzaz told us: Abdul-Warith bin Saeed told us: Amara told us, on the authority of Ikrimah, regarding his statement: Ta-Ha, he said: O man, speak to him in Nabataean. Ibn Hamid told us: Yahya bin Wadh told us: Abdullah told us, on the authority of Ikrimah, regarding his statement Ta-Ha, he said: In Nabataean: O human being. Muhammad bin Bashar told us: Abu Asim told us, on the authority of Qara bin Khalid, on the authority of Ad-Dahhak, regarding his statement, Ta-Ha, he said: O man, in Nabataean. Muhammad bin Bashar told us: Abd al-Rahman told us: Sufyan told us, on the authority of Hisayn, on the authority of Ikrimah, regarding his statement, Ta-Ha, he said: O man. Bishr told us, Qan: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada, his saying Ta-Ha he said: O man, and it is in Syriac. Al-Hasan told us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq told us, he said: Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada and al-Hasan, regarding his statement, Ta-Ha, they said: O man. It was narrated on the authority of Al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Muadh say: Ubayd told us, meaning Ibn Sulayman, who said: I heard Ad-Dahhak say regarding His statement, Ta-Ha, he said: O man. Others said: It is one of the names of God, and an oath by which God swore. Who said that? Ali told us, he said: Abdullah told us, he said: Muawiyah told us, on the authority of Ali, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding his statement Ta-Ha, he said: It is an oath by which God swore, and it is one of the names of God. Others said: It is alphabetical letters. Others said: It is separate letters, each of which indicates a meaning. They differed on that as they differed on the letter alif-lam-meem. We mentioned that in its places, and we explained that with its evidence. What I think is more correct than the sayings about it is the saying of the one who said: Its meaning is: O man, because it is a well-known word in ‘Ak, as far as I have been informed, and its meaning among them is: O man. I recited for Mutammam bin Nuwairah: A duck shouted in the battle but he did not answer, so I feared that he would be a stumbling block. Others said: Foolishness is one of your characteristics. May God not bless the cursed people. If this was known among them as we mentioned, then it is necessary to direct its interpretation to the meaning known among them, especially if it agrees with the interpretation of the scholars among the Companions and Followers.
20:2: Then the interpretation of the statement is: O man, We did not send down the Qur’an to you to make you miserable. We did not send it down to you to burden you with work beyond your ability. It was mentioned that this was said to him because of the fatigue, hardship, and staying up late at night that he was experiencing. Who said that? Muhammad ibn Amr told me, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, and Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us, both on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, We have not sent down the Qur’an to you to make you miserable. He said: It is like His saying, So recite what is easy for you of it (al-Muzzammil 73:20). So they would hang ropes around their chests during prayer. Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Husayn told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid, We have not sent down the Qur’an to you to make you miserable. He said in prayer, like His saying, So recite as much of it as is easy for you. (al-Muzzammil 73:25), so they would hang ropes on their chests in prayer. Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada: We did not send down the Qur’an to you to make you miserable. No, by God, God did not make it miserable, but He made it a mercy and a light, and a guide to Paradise.
20:3: And His saying, Except as a reminder for whoever fears, God Almighty says: We have not sent down this Qur’an to you except as a reminder for whoever fears God’s punishment, so he guards himself against it by performing the duties of his Lord and avoiding His prohibitions. As Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada, his statement, Except as a reminder for him who fears, and God sent down His books and sent His messengers as a mercy with which God has mercy on His servants, so that the one who remembers may remember, and a man may benefit from what he can of the Book of God, and it is a reminder for him in which God sent down what is lawful and what is unlawful, so He said, A revelation from Him who created the earth and the high heavens (Ta-Ha: 4). Yunus told me, he said: Ibn Wahb told us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His statement, Except as a reminder for whoever fears, he said: What We revealed to you is a reminder for whoever fears. The meaning of the statement then is: O man, We have not sent down this Qur’an to you to make you miserable thereby. We have not sent it down except as a reminder for whoever fears. The Arabists differed about the reason for the accusative case of tadhkirah. Some of the grammarians of Basra said: “He said: except a reminder” instead of so that you may be miserable, so he made it: We have not sent down the Qur’an to you except as a reminder. Some of the grammarians of Kufa said: It is accusative case based on We have not sent it down except as a reminder. Some of them rejected the saying of the speaker: It is accusative case instead of so that you may be miserable, and said: That is not permissible, because so that you may be miserable is in the denial, and except a reminder is in the confirmation, but it is a repetition. Some of them said: “The meaning of the statement is: We have not sent down the Qur’an to you except as a reminder for whoever fears,” not so that you may be miserable.
20:4: God Almighty says to His Prophet Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace: This Qur’an is a revelation from the Lord who created the earth and the high heavens. And high is the plural of high. The Arabists differed about the reason for the accusative case of his statement tanzilan. Some of the grammarians of Basra said: The accusative case means: God sent that down as a revelation. Some of those who denied that said that it is from two statements, but the meaning is: it is a revelation, then it was dropped and connected to the statement before it, so it came out of it and was not from its wording. Abu Jaafar said: Both statements are not wrong in my opinion.
20:5: And His saying, The Most Gracious is firmly established on the Throne? God Almighty says. He said: The Most Gracious is on His throne, raised and exalted. We have already explained the meaning of istiwaa with its evidence in the past, and we have mentioned the differences of those who differed about it, so that makes it unnecessary to repeat it in this place. There are two aspects to the subject of the word al-Rahman 55:One is in the meaning of His statement: a revelation, so the meaning of the statement is: He sent it down from the creation of the earth and the heavens, the Most Gracious sent it down, who established Himself on the Throne. The other is in His statement: He established Himself on the Throne, because in His statement established Himself, there is a mention of the Most Gracious.
20:6: God Almighty says: To God belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them, and whatever is under the soil, He owns it, and He is the Manager of all of it and the Disposer of all of it. By soil He means dew. Wet, damp soil is called: deficient soil. It is said from it: I enriched the earth, deficient soil. And soil is a source. And in a similar manner to what we said about that, the people of interpretation said. Who said that? Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada, his statement, and what is under the soil, and soil is: everything that is wet. It was narrated on the authority of Al-Husayn bin Al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Muadh say: Ubayd told us, who said: I heard Al-Dahhak say regarding His statement, and what is beneath the soil, that is, what is dug from the wet soil, and what he meant by that is: and what is beneath the seven earths. Like what Muhammad bin Ibrahim Al-Salimi, known as Ibn Sadran, told me. He said: Abu Asim told us. He said: Muhammad bin Rafa’ah told us, on the authority of Muhammad bin Ka’b: And what is under the soil. He said: The soil is seven earths.
20:7: God Almighty says: And whether you speak aloud, O Muhammad, or keep it quiet, it is all the same before your Lord, to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. For He knows the secret. He says: For nothing is hidden from Him that you conceal in your soul, that you have not revealed with your limbs, nor spoken with your tongue, nor uttered? And what is more hidden? Then the people of interpretation differed about the meaning of his saying, and concealed. Some of them said: Its meaning is: and concealed from the secret. He said: What is concealed from the secret is what a person tells himself and does not know it. Who said that? Ibn Hamid told us: Hakam told us, on the authority of Amr, on the authority of Ata’, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubair, on the authority of Ibn Abbas: He knows the secret and what is more hidden. He said: The secret is what you know, and what is more hidden is what God has cast into your heart that you did not do. Muhammad bin Saad told me, he said: My father told me, he said: My uncle told me, he said: My father told me, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, his statement, He knows the secret and what is more hidden, meaning by what is more hidden: what he did not do, and he does it. As for the secret: it means what he kept secret in himself. Ali told me, he said: Abdullah told us, he said: Muawiyah told us, on the authority of Ali, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding his statement, He knows the secret and what is more hidden, he said: The secret is what the son of Adam keeps secret in his soul. And what is more hidden is what the son of Adam conceals of what he is going to do before he does it, so God knows that, so His knowledge of what has passed of that and what remains is one knowledge, and all of creation with Him in that is like one soul, and that is His statement, He did not create you and resurrect you except as one soul (Luqman 31:28). Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, he said: Ibn Jurayj said, Saeed bin Jubair said, on the authority of Ibn Abbas: The secret is what a person keeps secret in his soul, and concealed is what a person does not know of what will happen. Zakariya bin Yahya bin Abi Zaida and Muhammad bin Amr told me: Abu Asim told us, on the authority of Isa, and Al-Harith told me: Al-Hasan told us: Warqa’ both told us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, regarding the statement of God, He knows the secret and what is more hidden, he said: More hidden means whispering. Ibn Amr and Al-Harith added in their hadiths: The secret is the action that people keep secret. Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid, and he concealed he said: the whispering. Hanad told us, he said: Abu Al-Ahwas told us, on the authority of Samak, on the authority of Ikrimah, regarding his statement, He knows the secret and what is more hidden, he said: The most hidden of your inner thoughts. Ibn Bashar told us: Al-Husayn ibn Al-Hasan Al-Ashqar told us: Abu Kudayna told us, on the authority of Ata’, on the authority of Saeed ibn Jubayr, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding his statement, He knows the secret and what is even more hidden, he said: The secret is what is in your soul today. And what is even more hidden is what will be tomorrow and the day after, and none knows it except God. Others said: Rather, its meaning is: And more hidden than the secret is what your soul does not tell you. Who said that? Al-Fadl bin Al-Sabah told us: Ibn Fadil told us, on the authority of Ata’, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubair, regarding his statement, He knows the secret and what is more hidden, he said: The secret is what you keep secret in your soul, and what is more hidden than that is what you do not tell yourself. Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada: And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and what is even more hidden. We used to say that the secret is what your soul speaks to you, and that what is even more hidden than the secret is what is to come that you have not spoken to yourself. Muhammad bin Bashar told us, he said: Sulayman bin Harb told us, he said: Hilal told us, he said: Abu Qatada told us, regarding His statement, He knows the secret and what is more hidden, he said: He knows what you keep secret in your soul, and what is more hidden: what was not and is yet to come. Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us: Abd al-Razzaq told us: Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada, regarding his statement, He knows the secret and what is more hidden, he said: More hidden than the secret is what your soul has told you, and what your soul has not told you of what is to come. It was narrated on the authority of Al-Husayn ibn Al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Muadh, who said: Ubayd told us, who said: I heard Ad-Dahhak say regarding His statement, He knows the secret and what is more hidden. As for the secret: it is what you keep secret in your soul. As for what is more hidden than the secret: it is what you did not do while you are doing it. God knows all of that. Others said: Rather, the meaning of this is that He knows the secret of the servants, but He has hidden His own secret and has not revealed it to anyone. Who said that? Yunus told me, he said: Ibn Wahb told us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His statement, He knows the secret and what is more hidden, he said: He knows the secrets of the servants, and He has hidden His secret, so He does not know. Abu Ja`far said: Those who interpreted this to mean that a secret is what a person tells someone else in secret. And that akhfa means what he tells himself. They interpreted akhfa to mean hidden. Some of them said: Af`al can be used in place of the subject, and they cited as evidence for their statement the poet’s saying: Men wished that I would die, and if I die, then that is a path in which I am not alone. The correct statement about this is the statement of those who said: Its meaning is: He knows the secret and what is more hidden than the secret, because that is the apparent meaning of the statement. If the meaning of that was what Ibn Zayd interpreted it, the statement would be: And God concealed His secret, because akhfa is a transitive verb, since it has the meaning of fa’ala according to what Ibn Zayd interpreted it to be. And in the isolation of akhfa is its object, and what works on it if it had the meaning of fa’ala is the clear evidence that it has the meaning of fa’ala. And the interpretation of the statement is: He knows the secret and what is more hidden than it. So since that is its interpretation, then the correct statement about the meaning of akhfa’ min al-sarr is to say: It is what God knows of what He concealed from His servants, and they did not know of what is and has not been, because what is apparent and was is not a secret, and what was not and is not being is nothing, and what was not and is being is more hidden than the secret, because no one knows that except God, then who among His servants informed Him of that.
20:8: As for the saying of the Most High, God, there is no god but He, He means by it: the One to be worshipped, to whom worship is not valid except. He says, So worship Him, O people, without any other gods or idols. “To Him belong the best names.” The Most High says: To your worshipped One, O people, belong the best names. He said: the best, so He made it singular, and it is a description of the names. He did not say the best, because the names are applied to these, so it is said: these are names, and this is in one word. From this is the saying of Al-A’sha: And if I find him, he will be followed by a forgiving Lord and pure, white women. So he used the word dhat alone, and it is an adjective for the eggs because this falls on them, as He said, Gardens of delight (al-Naml 27:60) and from this is the saying of the Most High, Other places (Ta-Ha 20:18). So he used the word akhra alone, and it is an adjective for marib, and marib is a plural, its singular is maribah, and he did not say akhr, for what we described. If he had said akhr, it would have been correct.
20:9: God Almighty says to His Prophet Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, comforting him from the hardship he is facing from the polytheists of his people, and informing him of what will happen to him and theirs, and that He is superior to them, and weakens the plot of the disbelievers, and He urges him to be serious in his matter, and to be patient in his worship, and to remember, in what befalls him from his enemies from the polytheists of his people and others, and in what he is doing of striving in his obedience, what befell his brother Moses, may God bless him and grant him peace, from his enemy, then from his people, and from the Children of Israel, and what he faced in it of affliction and hardship as a young child, then as a grown-up adult, then as a full-fledged man, And did there come to you, O Muhammad, the story of Moses Ibn Imran, when he saw a fire? He mentioned that this was in the winter at night, and that Moses had lost his way, so when he saw the light of the fire, he said to his family what he said.
20:10: Who said that: Musa bin Harun told us, he said: Amr told us, he said: Asbat told us, on the authority of Al-Suddi, on the authority of Abu Malik, and on the authority of Abu Salih, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, he said: When Moses had fulfilled his term, he traveled with his family on the best road. Abdullah bin Abbas said: It was winter, and a fire was raised for them, and when he saw it, he thought it was fire, but it was from the light of God. So he said to his family, ‘Stay here; I have perceived a fire.’ Ibn Humayd narrated: Salamah narrated to us, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq, on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih al-Yamani, who said: When Moses had fulfilled his term, he went out with his sheep, and with him his flint, and his staff in his hand, with which he would frighten his sheep during the day. When evening came, he would light a fire with his flint and spend the night by it with his family and his sheep. When morning came, he would be with his family and his sheep, and he would lean on his staff. When the night came, in which God wanted to honor Moses and initiate him with his prophethood and speech, he lost his way so that he did not know where to go. He took out his flint to light a fire for his family so that they would spend the night by it until morning, and he would know the direction of his path. He straightened his flint but could not kindle a fire for himself, and he struck until he was exhausted. The fire appeared and he saw it. “So he said to his family, ‘Stay here, for I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I can bring you a torch from it or find at the fire some guidance.’” He meant by his saying: I found a fire that he found it. One of the proverbs of the Arabs is after the rising of Inasa. It is also said: after the rising of Inasa, which is taken from Uns. And his saying, Perhaps I can bring you a torch from it, means: Perhaps I can bring you from the fire that you have warmed with a flame. A torch is the fire at the end of a stick or reed. The speaker says to his companion: Bring me a torch, and he gives it to him at the end of a stick or reed. And what Moses meant by his saying to his family, Perhaps I can bring you a torch from it, is perhaps I can bring you that so that you may warm yourself with it. As Ibn Hamid told us, he said: Salamah told us, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq, on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih, Perhaps I will bring you a torch from it. He said: A torch to warm yourselves with. His saying, Or I find guidance to the Fire, is an indication of the path that we have led astray, either from the report of a guide who guides us to it, or from a statement and knowledge by which we can discern and know it. And in a similar manner to what we said about that, the people of interpretation said. Who said that? Ali told me, he said: Abdullah told us, he said: Muawiyah told us, on the authority of Ali, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, his statement, Or I find guidance to the Fire, meaning: someone who shows the way. Muhammad bin Amr told me, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, and Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us both, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, regarding the statement of God, Or I find guidance for the Fire, he said: A guide who shows him the way. Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid, the same. Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us on the authority of Qatada, his statement, Or I find guidance on the Fire: meaning guides who show him the way. Ahmad bin Al-Muqaddam told me, he said: Al-Mu’tamir told us, he said: I heard my father narrating, on the authority of Qatada, on the authority of a companion of his, on the hadith of Ibn Abbas, that he claimed that it was a deer, or I find guidance on the fire. My father said: Qatada claimed that it was guidance on the road. Al-Hasan told us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq told us, he said: Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada, regarding his statement, Or I find guidance for the Fire, he said: Who will guide me to the path. Ibn Hamid told us: Salamah told us, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq, on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih: Or I find guidance for the Fire. He said: Guidance from the knowledge of the path that led us astray with a description of the report. Yunus told me, he said: Sufyan told us, on the authority of Abu Saeed, on the authority of Ikrimah, he said: Ibn Abbas said: Perhaps I will bring you a torch from it, or find guidance at the fire. He said: They had gone astray from the path, so he said: Perhaps I will find someone to show me the path, or I will bring you a torch so that you may warm yourself.
20:11: God Almighty says: So when Moses came to the fire,
20:12: His Lord called to him, O Moses, I am your Lord, so take off your shoes. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq, on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: Moses went out towards it, meaning towards the fire, and it was in a bramble tree, and some of the People of the Book say in a bramble bush. So when he approached, it held back from him. So when he saw it holding back, he turned away from it, and he felt fear in himself of it. So when he wanted to turn back, it approached him and then he spoke from the tree. So when he heard the voice, he felt reassured, and God, the Blessed and Exalted, said, O Moses, take off your shoes, for you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa. So he took them off and threw them away. Scholars differed about the reason why God ordered Moses to take off his sandals. Some of them said: He ordered him to do that because they were made of the skin of a dead donkey, and he did not want to step on the sacred valley with them, and he wanted to touch the valley’s pool. Who said that? Muhammad bin Bashar told us: Abd al-Rahman told us: Sufyan told us, on the authority of Asim, on the authority of Abu Qilabah, on the authority of Ka’b, that he saw them taking off their sandals, Take off your sandals, for you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa. He said: They were made of the skin of a dead donkey, and God wanted the sacred to touch them. Ibn Hamid told us: Yahya bin Wadh told us: Al-Hussein told us, on the authority of Yazid, on the authority of Ikrimah, regarding his statement, Then take off your shoes, he said: They were made of the skin of a dead donkey. Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saad told us, on the authority of Qatada, he said: He told us, that his shoes were made of donkey skin, so he took them off and then came to him. Al-Hasan told us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq told us, he said: Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada, regarding his statement, Then take off your shoes, he said: They were made of donkey skin, so he was told to take them off. Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Husayn told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, he said: And Umar ibn Ata’ informed me, on the authority of Ikrimah and Abu Sufyan, on the authority of Samar, on the authority of Jabir al-Ja’fi, on the authority of Ali ibn Abi Talib, Then take off your shoes. He said: They were made of donkey skin, so he was told to take them off. He said: And Qatada said something similar. Others said: They were made of cowhide, but God wanted Moses to step on the ground with his feet, so that its blessing would reach him. Who said that? Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Husayn told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, he said: Ibn Jurayj said, Al-Hasan said: They - meaning Moses' sandals - were made of cows, but God only wanted his feet to touch the blessing of the earth, and it had been sanctified twice. Ibn Jurayj said: It was said to Mujahid: They claimed that his sandals were made of donkey skin or the skin of a dead animal. He said: No, but he was commanded to touch the blessing of the earth with his feet. Yaqub told me, he said: Abu Bishr said, meaning Ibn Ulayyah, I heard Ibn Abi Nujayh say regarding his statement, Then take off your shoes, for you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa, he said: He says: Put your feet into the pond of the valley. Abu Jaafar said: The more correct of the two opinions on this matter is the opinion of the one who said: God Almighty commanded him to take off his shoes so that he could touch the valley’s blessing with his feet, as it was a sacred valley. We said that this is the more correct of the two interpretations, because there is no indication in the apparent meaning of the revelation that he ordered him to take them off because they were made of donkey skin or because they were impure, and there is no report of that from someone whose statement is binding as evidence. And in his statement, You are in the sacred valley, following it, there is clear evidence that he only ordered him to take them off for the reasons we mentioned. Even if the report that Bishr told us: Khalaf bin Khalifa told us, on the authority of Hamid bin Abdullah bin Al-Harith, on the authority of Ibn Masoud, on the authority of the Prophet of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, who said: On the day God concealed Moses, he was wearing a woolen cloak, a woolen cloak, woolen trousers, and sandals made of donkey skin that had not been slaughtered properly. We did not attribute it to anyone else, but there is a problem with its chain of transmission that must be verified. The reciters differed in their reading of His statement, Indeed, I am your Lord. Some of the reciters of Medina and Basra read it as It was called, O Moses, anī with the fathah on the alif of anī, because according to their reading it is in the nominative case with his statement: It was called, because its meaning is: This statement was called to them. Some of the general reciters of Medina and Kufa read it with the kasrah: It was called, O Moses, I, as a beginning, and the meaning of that is it was said: O Moses, I. Abu Ja`far said: The first reading is the more correct in our view, because the call has come between it and the action in that his saying, O Moses, and the point of his saying, He was called, is that it would have been used in that if it had been before his saying, O Moses, and that is to say, He was called, ‘O Moses, I am your Lord,’ and it has no point in that that comes after Moses. As for his saying, Indeed, you are in the sacred valley, he is saying, Indeed, you are in the purified, blessed valley. As Ali told me, he said: Abdullah told us, he said: Muawiyah told us, on the authority of Ali, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, his statement, Indeed, you are in the sacred valley, meaning: the blessed one. Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, he said: Mujahid said, his statement, Indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa, he said: It is sanctified and blessed twice. Yunus told me, he said: Ibn Wahb told us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His statement, Indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa, he said: In the blessed valley. The people of interpretation differed in their interpretation of his saying: He folded it. Some of them said: Its meaning is: You folded it in the sacred valley. According to this saying, from their saying folded a source came out from other than its wording, as if he said: I folded the sacred valley folded. Who said that? Muhammad bin Saad told me, he said: My father told me, he said: My uncle told me, he said: My father told me, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, his statement, Indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa, meaning the sacred land, and that is because he passed through its valley at night and he crossed it. It is said: I crossed such-and-such valley, Tuwa at night, and he ascended to the top of the valley, and that was the Prophet of God, Moses, may God bless him and grant him peace. Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is: twice. He said: His Lord called him twice. According to the saying of these people, tawa is also a source without its wording, and that is because its meaning according to them is: He was called, O Moses, twice, two calls. And some of them used to recite as evidence for his saying tawa that it means twice, the saying of Adi bin Zaid al-Abbadi: O you who criticize, sleep is not in its true nature, it is a fold of your hesitant delusion Others narrated this: Ali Thana: meaning one time after another. They said: Tawa and Thana have the same meaning. Who said that? Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada: So take off your shoes, for you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa. We were told that it was a valley that was sacred twice, and that its name was Tuwa. Others said: Rather, the meaning of this is: He was sanctified and folded twice. Who said that? Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, he said: Ibn Jurayj said, Al-Hasan said: He was sanctified twice. Others said: Rather, Tawa is the name of the valley. Who said that? Ali bin Dawud told me, he said: Abdullah told us, he said: Muawiyah told us, on the authority of Ali, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, his saying: Tuwa: the name of the valley. Muhammad bin Amr told me, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, and Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us, both of them, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid: Tuwa: he said: the name of the valley. Yunus told me, he said: Ibn Wahb told us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His statement, In the sacred valley of Tuwa, he said: That valley is Tuwa, where Moses was, and where what he had from God was. He said: It is towards the mountain. Others said: Rather, it was an order from God to Moses to step into the valley with his feet. Who said that? Muhammad bin Mansour Al-Tusi told us: Salih bin Ishaq told us, on the authority of Jaafar bin Burqan, on the authority of Ikrimah, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding the statement of God Almighty, “So take off your shoes. Indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa,” he said: He stepped into the valley. Ibn Hamid told us, he said: Yahya told us, he said: Al-Hasan told us, on the authority of Yazid, on the authority of Ikrimah, regarding his statement He folded he said: He trampled the valley. Muhammad ibn Amr told us, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, and Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us, both on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Saeed ibn Jubayr, regarding the statement of God, He folded up, he said: He trod the earth barefoot, as you enter the Kaaba barefoot, he said: from the blessing of the valley. Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid: Tawa means to step on the ground barefoot. The readers differed in their reading of this. Some of the readers of Medina read it as Tawa with a damma on the ta and leaving out the tanween, as if they made it the name of the land in which the valley is located, as the poet said: They supported their prophet and strengthened his resolve with Hanin when the heroes were helpless. So he did not make Hunayn a noun, because he made it the name of the town, not the valley. If he had made it the name of the valley, he would have made it a noun as the reciters read: And on the day of Hunayn, when your great number pleased you (al-Tawbah 9:25), and as the other said: Are we not the most honorable of the two heavy burdens in terms of travel and the greatest of them in terms of fire in the valley of Hira? He did not make Hira', which is a mountain, a noun, because he made it the name of the town. Likewise, Tawa in the reading of those who did not make it a noun, made it a name for the land. The majority of the readers of Kufa read it as Tawa with a damma on the ta' and the tanween, and the readers of that also differed in its meaning, as I mentioned about the differences of the people of interpretation. As for those who meant by it the source of Tawyit, there is no difficulty in making it a noun. As for those who wanted to make it a name for the valley, they only make it a noun because it is a masculine noun, not a feminine one, and the lam of the verb is a ya', so that made it lighter, so he made it a noun, as God said, And the day of Hunayn, since Hunayn was the name of a valley, and the valley is masculine. Abu Ja`far said: The more correct of the two opinions in my opinion is the reading of the one who reads with the damma of the ta’ and the tanween, because if it is the name of the valley, then it is entitled to the tanween, as mentioned before regarding the reason for the one who said that, because it is a verbal noun or an explanatory word, so also its ruling is the tanween, and in my opinion it is the name of the valley. Since that is the case, then it is in the accusative case in response to the valley.
20:13: The readers differed in reading this, so the majority of the readers who read it read it as wa-na with a shaddah on the nun, and ana with a fathah on the alif of ana in response to: Nawa-ya-Musa, the meaning of the statement according to them was: Nawa-ya-Musa, I am your Lord, and I have chosen you, and this is the reading that the majority of the readers of Kufa read it. As for the majority of the readers of Medina and Basra and some of the people of Kufa, they read it as wa-na-ikhtara-ka with a light nun as a statement from God about Himself that He has chosen him. Abu Ja`far said: The correct thing to say about this, in my opinion, is that they are two readings, each of which has been recited by reciters of knowledge of the Qur’an, with their meanings being in agreement. So whichever of them the reciter recites, he is correct in it. The interpretation of the words: It was called out, We have chosen you, so We have selected you for Our message to whom We send you. “So listen to what is revealed.” He says: So listen to Our revelation that We reveal to you, and understand it, and act upon it.
20:14: I am God God Almighty says: I am the one who is worshipped and no one is worthy of worship except Him. There is no god but Me, so do not worship anyone other than Me, for there is no god for whom worship is permissible or appropriate except Me. So worship Me He says: So devote your worship to Me and not to everything that is worshipped other than Me. And establish prayer for My remembrance. The people of interpretation differed in their interpretation of this. Some of them said: The meaning of this is: Establish prayer for Me, for if you establish it, you will remember Me. Who said that? Muhammad bin Amr told me, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, and Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us, both on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, regarding his statement, Establish prayer for My remembrance, he said: When he prays, he remembers his Lord. Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid, regarding his statement, And establish prayer for My remembrance, he said: When a servant remembers his Lord. Others said: Rather, the meaning of this is: And establish prayer when you remember it. Who said that? Muhammad bin Bashar told us: Abu Asim told us: Sufyan told us, on the authority of Mughira, on the authority of Ibrahim, regarding his statement, And establish prayer for My remembrance, he said: He prays it when he remembers it. Ahmad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Wahb told me: My uncle Abdullah ibn Wahb told me: Yunus and Malik ibn Shihab told me: Sa`id ibn al-Musayyab told me, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers it. God said: Establish prayer for My remembrance. Al-Zuhri used to recite it: Establish prayer for My remembrance in the same way as fa`ala. Abu Ja`far said: The more correct of the two interpretations is the interpretation of the one who said: Its meaning is: Establish prayer so that you may remember Me in it, because that is the more apparent of its two meanings. If its meaning was: When you remember it, the revelation would have been: Establish prayer for your remembrance of it. And in His saying: for My remembrance there is clear evidence for the correctness of what Mujahid said in interpreting that. And if the reading that we mentioned from al-Zuhri was a widespread reading in the readings of the regions, then the interpretation of the one who interpreted it to mean: Establish prayer when you remember it would be correct. That is because al-Zuhri directed his reading Establish prayer for My remembrance with the alif, not with the addition, to Establish for its remembrance, because the ha and the alif were deleted, and they are intended in the speech to reconcile it with the rest of the beginnings of the verses, since they were with the alif and the fat-ha. And if someone were to say about this reading of Al-Zuhri that we mentioned about him, that Al-Zuhri intended by opening it to make it an addition of an alif in order to reconcile it with the beginnings of the verses before and after it, because he differed with his reading of that as well from those who read it with an addition, and he said: That is like the saying of a poet: I wander as I wander, then I go to my mother and the infusion quenches my thirst. He meant: To my mother, and as the Arabs say: O father and mother, and she meant: O my father and mother, and he had a say in that.
20:15: God Almighty says: The hour in which God will raise the creatures from their graves for the Day of Resurrection will be I almost hide it. So, all the readers of the Islamic countries read the word I almost hide it from myself with the damma of the alif, meaning: I almost hide it from myself, so that no one will find out about it. This is the interpretation of most scholars. Who said that? Ali told me, he said: Abdullah told us, he said: Muawiyah told us, on the authority of Ali, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, his saying I almost hide it means: I do not reveal it to anyone but myself. Muhammad bin Saad told me, he said: My father told me, he said: My uncle told me, he said: My father told me, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding his statement, The Hour is coming - I almost conceal it. He said: It will not come to you except suddenly. Ibn Bashar told us, he said: Abu Ahmad told us, he said: Sufyan told us, on the authority of Laith, on the authority of Mujahid, The Hour is coming, and I almost hide it. He said: From myself. Muhammad bin Amr told us, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, and Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us, both on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, regarding the statement of God, I almost concealed it, he said: from myself. Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid, the same. Ibn Hamid told us: Jarir told us, on the authority of Ata’ bin Al-Sa’ib, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubair, on the authority of Ibn Abbas: I almost hide it. He said: From myself. Abdul-A’la bin Wasil told me, he said: Muhammad bin Ubaid al-Tanafisi told us, he said: Ismail bin Abi Khalid told us, on the authority of Abu Salih, regarding his statement, I almost concealed it, he said: He concealed them from himself. Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada, his statement, I almost concealed it, and in some readings it is: I concealed it from myself. And by my life, God concealed it from the angels brought near, and from the prophets sent. Al-Hasan told us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq told us, he said: Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada, he said in some of the letters: The Hour is coming, I almost hide it. Others said: It is I almost hid it with the opening of the alif from I hid it meaning: I showed it. Who said that? Ibn Hamid told us: Yahya bin Wadh told us: Muhammad bin Sahl told us: A man asked me in the mosque about this verse: Two months passed, then a month, and the dolls were on two couches, hiding a cloud. I said: They appear. Then Warqa’ bin Iyas said, while he was behind me: Saeed bin Jubair recited it to me, I almost hide it, with the alif in the accusative case. It has been narrated from Saeed bin Jubair that it is in agreement with the statement of others who said: Its meaning is: I almost hide it from myself. He mentioned the narration about it: Ibn Bashar told us: Abd al-Rahman told us: Sufyan told us, on the authority of Ata’, on the authority of Saeed ibn Jubayr and Mansur, on the authority of Mujahid, who said: The Hour is coming, and I almost hide it. They said: From myself. Ubaid bin Ismail Al-Habbari told me: Ibn Fadil told us, on the authority of Ata bin Al-Saib, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubair: I almost hide it. He said: From myself. Abu Ja`far said: What is more deserving of the interpretation of the verse than the statement is the statement of those who said: Its meaning is: I almost hide it from myself because the interpretation of the people of interpretation came with that. And what was mentioned from Sa`id bin Jubayr about reading that with the opening of the alif is a reading that I do not permit reading with it because it is contrary to the reading of the argument that it is not permissible to contradict in what it came with according to widespread transmission. If he said: Why did you direct the interpretation of his story I almost hide it with the damma of the alif to the meaning: I almost hide it from myself, without directing it to the meaning: I almost reveal it, and you know that concealment in the speech of the Arabs has two meanings: one is showing, and the other is concealment, and that showing in this place is more similar to the meaning of speech, since concealment from itself is almost impossible for the listeners to mean, since it is impossible for someone to hide from himself something that he knows, and nothing is hidden from God, the Most High? It was said: The matter in that is contrary to what you thought, and we directed the meaning of I hide it with the damma of the alif to the meaning: I conceal it from myself, because the well-known meaning of concealment in the speech of the Arabs is: covering. It is said: I concealed the thing if I covered it. And those who directed its meaning to showing relied on a verse of Imru’ al-Qais ibn ‘Abis al-Kindi. It was narrated on the authority of Muammar bin Al-Muthanna that he said: Abu Al-Khattab recited to me, on the authority of his family in his country: If you bury the disease, we will not fear it, and if you start war, we will not sit back. With the damma of the nun from la nakhfahu, and its meaning is: we do not show it, so their reliance in directing the concealment in this place to the showing was on what they mentioned from their hearing of this verse, on what I described from the damma of the nun from nakhfahu. And the trustworthy recited to me on the authority of al-Farra’: If you bury the disease, we will not fear it. By opening the letter nun from nakhafahu from khafatuhu I akhfahu, and this is more correct because it is known from the speech of the Arabs. So if that is the case, and opening the letter alif from akhfatuhu is not permissible according to us for what we mentioned, then the other is proven and correct, which is that the meaning of that is: I almost hid it from myself. As for the correctness of the statement in this regard, it is that God, the Most High, mentioned Him, addressed them in the Qur’an based on what they knew of their speech and the way they spoke to each other. Since it was known in their speech that one of them would say, if he wanted to exaggerate in reporting that he had concealed something that was a secret to him: I almost concealed this matter from myself because of how much I was secretive about it, and if I could conceal it from myself, I would conceal it. He addressed them based on what they had been accustomed to in this regard in speech among themselves, and what they knew in their language. And statements other than what we have said have been made about this. We chose this statement over other statements because it is in agreement with the statements of the people of knowledge from the Companions and the Followers, since we did not permit disagreement with them, regarding what was widely said by them and came from them in a manner that cuts off the excuse. As for those who said something other than what we said about it, from those who said it in a way that was extracted from the speech of the Arabs, without attributing it to an imam from the Companions or the Followers, and in a way that the speech could be interpreted in a way other than its known meaning, then they differed among themselves about its meaning. Some of them said: It could be interpreted as: I want to hide it. He said: This is well-known in the language. He mentioned that it was narrated from the Arabs that they would say: Those are my companions upon whom revelation was almost sent down. He said: Its meaning is: I do not send revelation except upon them. He said: It was said: I almost leave my home: meaning I do not leave my home. He provided evidence with a verse that he recited for some poets: Almost, almost, and that is the best will if the past of childhood could be returned He said: He means by almost: she wanted. He said: So the meaning is: I want to hide it so that each interpreter will be rewarded for what he strives for. He said: And what is similar to that is the saying of Zaid al-Khayl: Quick to attack, he sharpens his weapon, and his horn barely breathes. He said: It is as if he said: So his horn does not breathe, otherwise the meaning is weak. He said: And Dhu al-Raqqa said: If the flute changes the lovers, the trumpet of love will hardly leave the love of Mayya He said: The meaning is not: He had hardly left: that is, after ease, and he left after difficulty. Rather, the meaning is: He had not left, or he did not intend to leave, otherwise the meaning would be weak. He said: And likewise the saying of Abu al-Najm: If report of death reaches you, mourn for a father who has almost been overtaken by enemies and calamities. He said: The meaning is: The enemies have been defeated, otherwise it would not be praise if he intended to almost do and did not intend to do. Others said: Rather, the meaning of this is: The Hour is almost coming. He said: And the report ended with his saying: I am almost because its meaning is: I am almost bringing it. He said: Then he began and said: But I conceal it so that every soul may be rewarded for what it strives for. He said: And this is similar to the saying of Ibn Dabi’: I intended to do it but did not, and I almost did. I wish I had left it to Uthman’s relatives to cry over. He said: I almost did it, meaning: I almost did it. Others said: The meaning of I concealed it is to reveal it. They said: The Arabs have directed concealment and secrecy to the meaning of revelation. Some of them cited as evidence for his saying that the verse of Al-Farazdaq: When Hajjaj saw this, he drew his sword and captured the Haruri who had been hiding something. He said: What he meant by his saying: conceal is: show it. He said: It is possible that the meaning of his saying And they concealed their regret (Yunus 10:54) - (Saba’: 33) is and they showed it. He said: That is because they said: Oh, would that we could be sent back and not deny the signs of our Lord (al-An’am 6:27). All of those whose words we have mentioned said: It is possible that the words of the one who said: The meaning of that is: I almost conceal it from myself, is: He meant to conceal it from me and from myself. All of these statements that we have mentioned from those we have mentioned are a direction from them to the speech in a direction other than its known meaning, and it is not permissible to direct the meanings of the speech of God in a direction other than the most prevalent among those addressed by it. In that, along with their disagreement with the interpretation of the people of knowledge, there is just evidence of the error of what they have gone to in it. And His statement, That every soul may be rewarded for what it strives for, the Most High says: The Hour will come so that every soul may be rewarded. He says: That every soul that its Lord has tested with worship in this world may be rewarded for what it strives for. He says: for what it does of good and evil, obedience and disobedience.
20:16: And His statement, So let not he who does not believe in it turn you away from it, God Almighty says: So let not he who does not believe in it turn you away, O Moses, from preparing for the Hour, meaning: he who does not acknowledge the occurrence of the Hour, nor believe in the resurrection after death, nor hope for reward, nor fear punishment. And His statement, And follows his desire, means: he follows his own desire, and disobeys God's command and prohibition. So you will perish, means: you will perish if you turn away from preparing for the Hour, and from believing in it, and that God will raise up creation for its occurrence from their graves after their annihilation, by turning away from those who disbelieve in it. Some of them claimed that the ha’ and the alif in His statement So let them not avert you from it are a metaphor for mentioning faith. He said: Rather, it was said about it and it is a metaphor for faith, just as it was said Indeed, your Lord, after that, is Forgiving and Merciful (al-A’raf 7:53) and (al-Nahl 16:110 and 119). It refers to the action, and faith was not mentioned in this place, so that is considered from its mention. Rather, the mention of the Hour occurred, so it is more appropriate for it to be from its mention.
20:17: God Almighty says: What is this in your right hand, O Moses? The ba’ in His statement in your right hand is a connection to that, and the Arabs connect that and this as they connect the ladi, and from this is the saying of Yazid bin Mufrij: Lentils, what do you have over the servants of the Emirate? I have secured you, and this is what you are carrying, free As if he said: The one you are carrying is divorced. Perhaps someone might say: What is the reason for God asking Moses about what was in his hand? Did he not know that what was in his hand was a staff? It was said to him: That is not what you thought, and the Almighty said that to him when He wanted to turn it into a snake that moved, and it was a piece of wood, so He alerted him to it and confirmed to him that it was a piece of wood that he could lean on and use to herd his sheep, to show him His power over whatever He wills, the greatness of His authority, and the implementation of His command in whatever He liked by turning it into a snake that moved, if He wanted that for him, to make that a sign for Moses along with all His signs to Pharaoh and his people.
20:18: God Almighty says, informing us about Moses: Moses said, answering his Lord, It is my staff; I lean on it and beat down leaves with it for my sheep. He says, I strike the dry tree with it so that its leaves fall and my sheep graze them. It is said from this: So-and-so beat the tree, beating it up, if he beats the leaves of its branches so that its leaves fall, as the rajaz poet said: I beat my sheep with a stick from the soft arak and bisham trees And in a similar manner to what we said about that, the people of interpretation said. Who said that? Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us: Abd al-Razzaq told us: Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada, regarding his statement, And I beat with it my sheep, he said: I beat with it the trees. Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada, or I drive it to my sheep, he said: I beat it. Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada, And I would brush my sheep with it. He said: The Prophet of God, Moses, peace be upon him, would brush tree leaves for his sheep. Musa told me, he said: Amr told us, he said: Asbat told us, on the authority of Al-Suddi: And I beat the trees with it for my sheep, meaning: I beat the trees with it for the sheep, and the leaves fall. Yunus told me, he said: Ibn Wahb told us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding his statement, It is my staff; I lean on it and beat down leaves with it for my sheep, he said: He leans on it when he walks with the sheep, and beats down leaves with it, shaking the trees until the leaves, ropes, and other things fall. Ibn Hamid told us: Yahya bin Wadh told us: Al-Hasan told us, on the authority of Ikrimah: And I strike the trees with it, and their leaves fall on me. He said: I strike the trees with it, and their leaves fall on me. Abdullah bin Ahmed bin Shabwayh told me, he said: Ali bin Al-Hassan told us, he said: Hussein told us, he said: I heard Ikrimah say: And I strike the trees with it, so the leaves fall on my sheep. He said: I strike the trees with it, so the leaves fall on my sheep. It was narrated on the authority of Al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Muadh say: Ubayd narrated to us, who said: I heard Al-Dahhak say regarding His statement, And I beat with it my sheep, meaning: I beat with it the trees until what my sheep eat falls from them. And his saying, And I have other needs in it, means: I have other needs in this staff of mine, and it is the plural of ma’ribah, and there are three dialects for it in the Arab dialects: ma’ribah with a damma on the ra, “ma’ribah” with a fatha, and ma’ribah with a kasra. It is a passive participle from their saying, I have no need for this matter, meaning, I have no need for it. And it was said, other, and they are plural ma’rib, and he did not say another, just as it was said, To Him belong the best names (Ta-Ha: 8) - (al-Hashr 59:24). And I explained the reason for explaining that there. And similar to what we said about the meaning of goals, the people of interpretation said. Who said that? Ahmad bin Abda Al-Dhabi told us: Hafs bin Jami’ told us: Samak bin Harb told us, on the authority of Ikrimah, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding his statement, And I have other needs therein, he said: Other needs that I know of. Ali told me, he said: Abdullah told us, he said: Muawiyah told us, on the authority of Ali, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, his saying and I have other interests in it is like saying other needs. Muhammad bin Amr told me, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid: And I have other interests in it. He said: Needs. Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us, both of them, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, And I have other interests in it. He said: Needs and benefits. Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid: And I have other interests in it. He said: Needs. Musa told us, he said: Amr bin Hammad told us, he said: Asbat told us, on the authority of Al-Suddi: And I have other needs in it, meaning: other needs for which I carry the baggage and the water skin. Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada: And I have other interests in it. He said: Other needs. Al-Hasan told us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq told us, he said: Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada, regarding his statement, And I have other interests therein, he said: Other needs and benefits. Ibn Hamid told us: Salamah told us, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq, on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih: And I have other interests in it: meaning other benefits. Yunus told me, he said: Ibn Wahb told us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding his statement, And I have other needs therein, he said: Other needs besides that. It was narrated on the authority of Al-Hussein, who said: I heard Abu Muadh say: Ubaid narrated to us, who said: I heard Al-Dahhak say regarding his statement, other purposes, he said: other needs.
20:19: God Almighty says: God said to Moses: Throw down your staff that is in your right hand, O Moses. God Almighty says: So Moses threw it down, and God made it a serpent that moved. Before that, it was a dry piece of wood, a staff that he leaned on and used to frighten his sheep with, so it became a serpent by God’s command.
20:20: Ahmad bin Abdah Al-Dhabi narrated to us, he said: Hafs bin Jami' narrated to us, he said: Samak bin Harb narrated to us, on the authority of Ikrimah, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, he said: When it was said to Moses: Throw it, O Moses, he threw it, and behold, it was a serpent, darting about, and it had not been a serpent before that. He said: It passed by a tree and ate it, and passed by a rock and swallowed it. He said: Moses began to hear the sound of the rock in its belly. He said: So he turned away, and it was called, O Moses, take it, but he did not take it. Then it was called a second time: Take it and fear not, but he did not take it. Then it was said to him a third time: Indeed, you are among those who are secure (al-Qasas 28:31), so he took it. Musa bin Harun told me, he said: Amr told us, he said: Asbat told us, on the authority of Al-Suddi, he said: His Lord said to him, meaning to Moses, Throw it down, O Moses, meaning So he threw it down and behold, it was a serpent, darting about. “But when he saw it writhing as if it were a serpent, he turned in flight and did not look back.” (al-Naml 27:110) Then it was called, “O Moses, do not fear. Indeed, no messengers fear in My presence.” (al-Naml 27:110)
20:21: Ibn Hamid told us: Salamah told us, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq, on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih: He said, ‘Throw it down, O Moses.’ So he threw it down, and behold, it was a serpent, darting about. It quivered, with fangs and a form as God willed it to be. Then he saw a terrible thing, so he turned and fled, and did not look back. Then his Lord called to him: “O Moses, come forward and do not fear. We will restore it to its former state.” And His statement, He said, ‘Take it and do not fear,’ means that God Almighty said to Moses: Take the snake, and the ha and the alif are from the mention of the snake. And do not fear, meaning: Do not fear this snake. We will restore it to its former state, meaning: We will restore it to its former state before We made it a snake, and We will return it to a stick as it was. It is said to everyone who was doing something and then abandoned it, turned away from it, and then went back to it: So-and-so returned to his former state, returned to his former state, and returned to his former state. And in a similar manner to what we said about that, the people of interpretation said. Who said that? Ali told me, he said: Abdullah told us, he said: Muawiyah told us, on the authority of Ali, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, his saying her first life means: her first state. Muhammad bin Amr told me, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, and Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us, both on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, Her first life he said: Her appearance. Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid, the same. Ibn Hamid told us: Salamah told us, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq, on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih: We will restore it to its former state, meaning, we will restore it to its former state as it was. Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada: We will restore it to its former state. He said: To its former form.
20:22: God Almighty says: And close your hand, O Moses, and place it under your arm, and the two wings are the two hands, and this is how the story was narrated from Abu Hurairah and Kaab al-Ahbar. As for the Arabs, they say: They are the two sides. And some of them used as evidence for his saying that the words of the rajaz poet: I hug him to my chest and my wing And in a similar manner to what we said in the interpretation of that, the people of interpretation said. Who said that? Muhammad bin Amr told us, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, and Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us, both on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, his statement, to your side, he said: His hand is under his arm. Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Husayn told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid, similarly. And his saying, It comes out white without blemish, he mentioned that Moses, peace be upon him, was a dark-skinned man, so he put his hand in his pocket, then he took it out white without blemish, without leprosy, like snow, then he put it back, and it came out as it was, in its color. Ibn Hamid told us that. He said: Salamah told us, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq, on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih. Ismail bin Musa Al-Fazari told us: Sharik told us, on the authority of Yazid bin Abi Ziyad, on the authority of Muqsim, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding his statement, It comes out white without disease, he said: without leprosy. Muhammad bin Amr told us, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, and Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us, both of them, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, without any harm, he said: without leprosy. Al-Hasan told us: Abd al-Razzaq told us, on the authority of Muammar, on the authority of Qatada, regarding his statement, white without defect, he said: without leprosy. Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid, the same. Bishr told us, he said: Yazid told us, he said: Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada, without any harm, he said: without leprosy. Musa told us, he said: Amr told us, he said: Asbat told us, on the authority of Al-Suddi, It comes out white without any defect. He said: Without leprosy. It was narrated on the authority of Al-Husayn bin Al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Muadh say: Ubayd told us, who said: I heard Al-Dahhak say regarding His statement, without any harm, that he said: without leprosy. Ibn Bashar told us: Hammad ibn Mas`adah told us: Qurrah told us, on the authority of al-Hasan, regarding the statement of God, white without defect, he said: God brought it forth without defect, without leprosy, so Moses knew that he had met his Lord. And his statement, another sign, means: This is another sign and indication other than the sign that We showed you before it of the staff being transformed into a serpent that crawls about, based on the truth of the message We sent you with to whom We sent you. And the sign is placed in the accusative case because of its connection to the verb, since nothing appeared to raise it from this or it.
20:23: And His statement, That We may show you some of Our greatest signs, the Most High says: And fold your hand, O Moses, into your wing, and it will come out white without disease, that We may show you some of Our greatest proofs of the greatness of Our authority and power. And He said the greatest, so He made it singular? And He said, From Our signs, as He said, To Him belong the best names. (Ta-Ha: 8) (al-Hashr 59:24), and we have explained that there. And some of the people of Basra used to say: The greatest was only said because it was intended to be presented, and its meaning according to him was: That We may show you some of Our greatest signs.
20:24: God Almighty says to His Prophet Moses, peace be upon him: Go O Moses to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed. He says: He exceeded his limits and rebelled against his Lord. We have already explained the meaning of transgression in a way that makes it unnecessary to repeat it here. There is something omitted in the speech that is sufficient for the listener to understand what was mentioned of it, which is His saying, Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed. So call him to the Oneness of God and His obedience, and to send the Children of Israel with you.
20:25: He said, 'My Lord, expand my chest for me.' He said, My Lord, expand my chest for me, so that I may understand from You what You entrust to me of Your revelation, and with it I may dare to speak to Pharaoh.
20:26: And make my task easy for me He says: And make it easy for me to carry out the message that you have entrusted me with, and burden me with obedience. And in a similar manner to what we said about that, the people of interpretation said. Who said that? Yunus told me, he said: Ibn Wahb told us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding God’s statement, My Lord, expand my chest for me, he said: It is a boldness for me.
20:27: And his saying, And loosen the knot from my tongue, means: And loosen my tongue with speech, and there was in it, as he mentioned, a stutter about the speech that had been from his throwing the burning coal into his mouth on the day Pharaoh intended to kill him. He mentioned the narration of that on the authority of the one who said it: Muhammad ibn Amr told me, he said: Abu Asim told us, he said: Isa told us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Saeed ibn Jubayr, regarding his statement, A knot from my tongue, he said: It is a lump of burning coal that he put in his mouth on the command of Pharaoh’s wife, to repel Pharaoh’s punishment from him, when Moses took hold of his beard while he was not conscious, and he said: This is an enemy of mine, and she said to him: He is not sensible. Al-Harith told me, he said: Al-Hasan told us, he said: Warqa’ told us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, And untie the knot from my tongue is a burning coal that he put in his mouth on the authority of Pharaoh’s wife, to ward off Pharaoh’s punishment from him, when Moses took hold of his beard while he was not conscious, and he said: This is an enemy of mine, and she said to him: He is not conscious, this is the saying of Saeed bin Jubayr. Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, on the authority of Mujahid, regarding his statement, And untie the knot from my tongue, he said: A knot from a burning coal that he put in his mouth, on the authority of Pharaoh’s wife, to avert the punishment of Pharaoh when he took hold of his beard. Musa told us, he said: Amr told us, he said: Asbat told us, on the authority of Al-Suddi, he said: When the boy, meaning Musa, moved, his mother Asiya gave him to him as a boy, and while she was dancing and playing with him, she handed him to Pharaoh and said: Take him. When he took him to him, Musa took hold of his beard and plucked it, so Pharaoh said: Bring the slaughterers. Asiya said: Do not kill him; perhaps he may be of benefit to us, or we may adopt him as a son (al-Qasas 28:19). He is only a boy who does not understand, and he only did this from his childhood, and I know that there is no one in the people of Egypt sweeter than me. I put on him jewelry of rubies, and I put hot coals for him. If he takes the rubies, then he understands, so slaughter him, and if he takes the hot coals, then he is only a boy. So she brought out her rubies for him and put a basin of hot coals for him. Then Gabriel, peace be upon him, came and threw a hot coal in his hand, so Musa threw it in his mouth, and it burned his tongue. He is the one about whom God Almighty says: And untie the knot. From my tongue * they understand my speech.” So it was removed from Moses for that reason.
20:28: And his saying, They understand my words, means: They understand from me what I address them with and what I respond to them with.
20:29: And appoint for me a helper from among my family. He says: And appoint for me a helper from among my family.
20:30: Aaron, my brother. There are two aspects to the accusative case of Aaron: One of them is that Aaron is accusative as a translation of the minister. Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, he said: Ibn Abbas said: Aaron was older than Moses.
20:31: God Almighty says, informing us about Moses that he asked his Lord to strengthen his back with his brother Aaron. What he means by his saying strengthen my back with him is to strengthen my back, and I mean by him, it is said: So-and-so strengthened so-and-so: if he helped him and strengthened his back. And in a similar manner to what we said about that, the people of interpretation said. Who said that? Muhammad bin Saad told me, he said: My father told me, he said: My uncle told me, he said: My father told me, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ibn Abbas, his statement, Strengthen my back with it, meaning: Strengthen my back with it. Yunus told me, he said: Ibn Wahb told us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, in his statement, Strengthen my back with it, he said: Strengthen my affair with it, and strengthen me with it, for I have strength with it.
20:32: And his saying, And make him a partner in my affair, means: And make him a prophet just as you made me a prophet, and send him with me to Pharaoh.
20:33: So that we may glorify You much He says: So that we may magnify You by glorifying You much.
20:34: And we remember You often so we praise You.
20:35: You were ever watching us means: You were ever watching us, nothing of our actions was hidden from You. It was mentioned on the authority of Abdullah bin Abi Ishaq that he used to read ashdud bih azri with the opening of the alif of ashdud and ashrakhu fi amri with the closing of the alif of ashrakhu, meaning the report from Moses about himself that he would do that, not as a supplication. If it is read in this way, ashdud and ashrak are in the jussive mood as a reward or as an answer to the supplication. This is a reading that I do not see as a reading, even though it has an understandable meaning, because it is contrary to the reading of the proof that it is not permissible to contradict.
20:36: God Almighty says: God said to Moses, peace be upon him: You have been given what you asked of your Lord, O Moses, in expanding your chest, making your task easy for you, untying the knot from your tongue, making your brother Aaron your minister, strengthening your resolve with him, and making him a partner in the message with you.
20:37: And We have certainly bestowed favor upon you another time. God Almighty says: And We have certainly bestowed favor upon you, O Moses, before this time another time.
20:38: And that was when We revealed to your mother, when she gave birth to you in the year in which Pharaoh was killing every newborn male among your people, what We revealed to her. Then the Most High explained what He revealed to his mother, saying: It is to throw him into the chest. So the word that is in the accusative case in response to what is in His statement, what is revealed, and a translation of it.
20:39: God Almighty says: And We have already bestowed upon you, O Moses, another time when We inspired your mother, to throw your son Moses when she gave birth to you in the chest. Then throw him into the river, meaning by river: the Nile. And let the river cast him upon the shore. He says: Throw him into the river, the river casts him upon the shore, and it is a reward that was brought forth in the manner of a command, as if the river was the one commanded, as God Almighty said: Follow our way, and we will bear your sins (al-Ankabut 29:2) meaning: Follow our way, and we will bear your sins, so his mother did that to him, and the river cast him into the watering place of Pharaoh’s people. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq, who said: When Moses was born, his mother breastfed him, until when Pharaoh ordered the killing of the boys according to that tradition, she went to him and did with him what God Almighty had commanded her. She put him in a small chest and prepared it for him, then she went to the Nile and threw him in it. Pharaoh was sitting in a council of his, which he used to sit in on the bank of the Nile every morning. While he was sitting, the Nile passed by the chest and threw it out, and Asiyah, the daughter of Muzahim, his wife, was sitting beside him. He said: This is something in the sea, so bring it to me. His helpers went out to him and brought it. He opened the chest and there was a baby in his cradle. God instilled His love upon him and showed him His kindness. God Almighty meant by His saying, An enemy of Mine and an enemy of his will seize him. Pharaoh is the enemy, he was of God and of Moses. Musa told us, he said: Amr told us, he said: Asbat told us, on the authority of Al-Suddi, regarding his statement, Then throw him into the sea, which is the sea, which is the Nile. The people of interpretation differed regarding the meaning of the love that God Almighty said, And I bestowed upon you love from Me. Some of them said: He meant by that that He made him beloved to His servants. Who said that? Al-Husayn bin Ali Al-Sada’i and Al-Abbas bin Muhammad Al-Duri told me: Husayn Al-Ja’fi told us, on the authority of Musa bin Qabas Al-Hadrami, on the authority of Salamah bin Kuhail, regarding the statement of God, And I have bestowed upon you love from Me, Abbas said: I have made you beloved to My servants, and Al-Sada’i said: I have made you beloved to My creation. Others said: Rather, the meaning of this is: You have good character. Who said that? Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Hussein told us, he said: Ibrahim bin Mahdi told us, on the authority of a man, on the authority of Al-Hakam bin Abaan, on the authority of Ikrimah, regarding his statement, And I bestowed upon you love from Me, he said: Goodness and charm. Abu Ja`far said: What is more correct than what is said about this is that it is said: God cast His love upon Moses, as He, the Most High, said: And I cast upon you love from Me, so He made him beloved to Asiya, the wife of Pharaoh, until she adopted him, nurtured him, and raised him, and to Pharaoh, until he stopped his hostility and evil. And say! It is said: It is said: And I cast upon you love from Me because he made him beloved to everyone who saw him. The meaning of I cast upon you love from Me is I made you beloved to them. A man says to another if he loves him: I cast upon you my mercy, meaning my love. The least interpretation differed in the interpretation of the saying, And let it be made under My eyes. Some of them said: Its meaning is: And let it be nourished and raised on My love for Me and My will. Who said that? Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us: Abd al-Razzaq told us: Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada, regarding his statement: And that you may be nourished under My eyes, he said: It is his food and that you may be nourished under My eyes. Yunus told me, he said: Ibn Wahb told us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding his statement, And let it be made under My eyes, he said: He made him live in the king’s house, enjoying himself and being luxurious, and his food with them was the food of the king, so that was the craft. Others said: Rather, the meaning of this is: You are in my eyes in all your circumstances.
20:40: Who said that: Al-Qasim told us, he said: Al-Husayn told us, he said: Hajjaj told us, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, And let it be done under My eyes, he said: You are under My eyes when your mother put you in the chest, then in the sea, and when your sister walks. Ibn Nahik read and let it be done, with the ta’ open. And he interpreted it as follows: Ibn Hamid told us: Yahya bin Wadh told us: Abdul-Mumin told us: I heard Abu Nahik recite: And do it under my eyes. So I asked him about that, and he said: And do it under my eyes. Abu Ja`far said: The reading that I do not permit reading with any other than it is wal-tasna` with a damma on the ta’, due to the consensus of the authoritative reciters on it. If that is the case, then the most appropriate of the two interpretations is the interpretation that Qatada interpreted, which is And I have bestowed upon you love from Me and and that you may be nourished by My eyes, I have bestowed upon you love from Me.
